extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, authors, content creators, and anyone writing pitches/loglines for film, TV, short film, or books
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing a concise logline: a one-sentence (or very short) summary that captures a story's central conflict, hooks interest, and communicates the protagonist, goal, obstacles, and unique element. Useful for pitches, program guides, and marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — brief one-sentence summary stating central conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A log line or logline is a brief (usually one-sentence) summary of a television program, film, short film or book, that states the central conflict of the story, often providing both a synopsis of the story's plot, and an emotional "hook" to stimulate interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize central conflict and an emotional hook; keep it brief and summary-like rather than a full synopsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form/Length — usually a single sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-sentence program summary in TV Guide is a log line. "A log line is a single sentence describing your entire story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the logline to one sentence where possible (some sources allow one or two sentences), prioritizing concision and immediate clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus — capture the premise/main conflict (not a theme statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A logline is a one-sentence summary of the story's main conflict. It is not a statement of theme but rather a premise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write a thematic essay; make the central conflict/premise explicit. (Note: another cited view says a logline "goes to the heart... defining the theme ... and suggest[ing] a bigger meaning" — use sparingly if at all.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Three anchors — protagonist, want(s), and stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis is on what makes their property unique... the logline provides the content creator with a concise way to focus on the three main anchors of their writing: the protagonist, the protagonist's wants (goal(s) or desire(s)), and what is at stake (risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly name or imply the protagonist, their primary goal/desire, and what will be lost or gained (stakes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four facts to include — main character, goal, obstacles/villains, unique aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: A log line should contain four facts: "the main character, what the main character wants," the villain(s) or obstacle(s), "standing in the way," and, "the unique aspect(s) of the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the logline answers: Who is the main character? What do they want? Who/what blocks them? What makes this story distinct?

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative elements to reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative elements often referenced in a logline include the setting, protagonist, antagonist, inciting incident, and a conflict and a goal (the conflict's resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant and concise, indicate setting, the inciting incident that sparks the conflict, and the antagonist or opposing force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest change and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Change, such as character growth, and action should be suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imply an arc or transformation and show active stakes (what the protagonist must do), rather than only describing static circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — sell and demonstrate uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: A logline ... helps content creators simply and easily sell their work in a single sentence, because the emphasis is on what makes their property unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft the logline to be marketable: highlight the unique hook that differentiates the project from others in its genre.
